13-1

Lecture 13-1 · Differential (Rayleigh) distillation

When a charge is simply boiled and its vapour condensed, how do the residue and the distillate compositions change with time?

Lecture 13-1 · the plan

From one boiling pot to a cut sequence

  1. Why batch, and the simple stillfive reasons; Fig. 13.1
  2. The Rayleigh equationa moving species balance becomes $\ln(W/W_0)$ as an integral
  3. Closed forms and the average distillateconstant $K$ (13-4), constant $\alpha$ (13-5), $(x_D)_{avg}$ (13-6)
  4. Examples 13.1–13.3a constant-boilup run, tabulated vapour–liquid equilibrium (VLE), and how $\alpha$ sets purity
  5. Multicomponent form and the cut sequence(13-7)–(13-10); light-key (LK) cut, slop cut, heavy-key (HK) residue; then Problems 13.1–13.8

13-1 · why batch

Five situations where batch distillation wins

A continuous column runs one feed at steady state. Batch runs no steady state: a charge, a pot, compositions that drift.

1

Small capacity

Too little feed for continuous operation

2

Many feedstocks

One unit, seasonal or customer products

3

New products

Samples for potential buyers

4

Batch upstream

Feed varies batch to batch

5

Fouling feed

Solids, tars or resins would plug trays

13-1 · the Rayleigh equation

A balance on a pot that shrinksstep 1 of 3

The pot holds $Wx_W$ moles of a species. Vapour carries it away at $Dy_D$ — write that down.

$\dfrac{d}{dt}(Wx_W) = -Dy_D$the species leaves only in the vapour
$W\dfrac{dx_W}{dt} + x_W\dfrac{dW}{dt} = -Dy_D$(13-1)product rule: both $W$ and $x_W$ change
$W\,dx_W + x_W\,dW = y_D\,dW$multiply by $dt$; total balance gives $-D\,dt = dW$

Holds at any instant for any species — no equilibrium assumption yet.

13-1 · the Rayleigh equation

Separate and integrate from the chargestep 2 of 3

From step 1$W\,dx_W + x_W\,dW = y_D\,dW$
$W\,dx_W = (y_D - x_W)\,dW$collect the $dW$ terms on one side
$\dfrac{dx_W}{y_D-x_W} = \dfrac{dW}{W}$separate variables
$\displaystyle\int_{x_{W_0}}^{x_W}\frac{dx_W}{y_D-x_W} = \int_{W_0}^{W}\frac{dW}{W} = \ln\!\left(\frac{W}{W_0}\right)$(13-2)integrate from the charge $W_0,\ x_{W_0}$

Still general: $y_D$ needs a relation to $x_W$ before it can be integrated.

13-1 · the Rayleigh equation

One equilibrium stage closes itstep 3 of 3

(13-2)$\displaystyle\int_{x_{W_0}}^{x_W}\dfrac{dx_W}{y_D-x_W}=\ln\dfrac{W}{W_0}$
$\displaystyle\int_{x_0}^{x}\frac{dx}{y-x} = \ln\!\left(\frac{W}{W_0}\right)$(13-3)no reflux: $y_D=y$ in equilibrium with $x=x_W$
$\displaystyle\int_{x_0}^{x}\frac{dx}{(K-1)x}$close-boiling, constant $P$: $y=Kx$, $K$ constant
$\ln\!\left(\dfrac{W}{W_0}\right) = \dfrac{1}{K-1}\ln\!\left(\dfrac{x}{x_0}\right)$(13-4)integrate $dx/x$

$K$ = vapour–liquid ratio $y/x$; (13-4) fails once $K$ drifts with pot temperature.

13-1 · closed form for a binary

Constant $\alpha$: partial fractions do the work

$y=\dfrac{\alpha x}{1+(\alpha-1)x}\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{1}{y-x}=\dfrac{1+(\alpha-1)x}{(\alpha-1)\,x(1-x)}$insert the constant-$\alpha$ equilibrium curve (7-3)
$\dfrac{1}{y-x}=\dfrac{1}{\alpha-1}\left[\dfrac{1}{x}+\dfrac{\alpha}{1-x}\right]$partial fractions; check at $x\to0$ and $x\to1$
$\ln\!\left(\dfrac{W_0}{W}\right)=\dfrac{1}{\alpha-1}\left[\ln\!\left(\dfrac{x_0}{x}\right)+\alpha\ln\!\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1-x_0}\right)\right]$(13-5)integrate each term into (13-3)

$\alpha=\dfrac{y(1-x)}{x(1-y)}$, volatility of the light component relative to the heavy; valid while $\alpha$ is constant.

13-1 · what is in the receiver

The average distillate needs no integral

(13-5) gives the pot. The receiver collects everything that left, so an overall balance is enough.

$W_0x_0 = Wx + (W_0-W)\,(x_D)_{avg}$species balance: charge = residue + receiver
$(x_D)_{avg}=(y_D)_{avg}=\dfrac{W_0x_0-Wx}{W_0-W}$(13-6)solve for the receiver composition
$t=\dfrac{W_0-W}{V}$constant boilup and no reflux: $D=V$

$(x_D)_{avg}$ = mole fraction in the accumulated distillate; $t$ in h when $V$ in kmol/h.

13-1 · any two species $i$, $j$

The multicomponent Rayleigh equation

$M_i$
moles of species $i$ in the still pot, $Wx_{W_i}$
kmol
$\alpha_{i,j}$
relative volatility $y_{D_i}x_{W_j}/y_{D_j}x_{W_i}$, taken constant
–
$dM_i/dM_j = y_{D_i}/y_{D_j}$(13-7)divide the two balances $dM_i/dt=-Dy_{D_i}$
$dM_i/dM_j=\alpha_{i,j}\,(x_{W_i}/x_{W_j})$(13-8)replace the vapour ratio by $\alpha_{i,j}$
$dM_i/M_i=\alpha_{i,j}\,dM_j/M_j$(13-9)$x_{W_i}/x_{W_j}=M_i/M_j$: $W$ cancels
$\ln(M_i/M_{i_0})=\alpha_{i,j}\ln(M_j/M_{j_0})$(13-10)integrate from the charge

13-1 · from purity limits to an operating plan

Light key cut, slop cut, heavy key residue

Purity falls as more is vaporized, so the run is split into cuts, each stopped at an impurity limit.

1

LK cut

Until total distillate reaches its HK limit

2

Slop cut

Impure LK until the residue meets spec

3

HK residue

Empty the HK-rich residue

4

Recycle

Slop joins the next charge

LK = more volatile key, HK = less volatile key. Lower $\alpha_{LK,HK}$: larger slop cut.

Problem 13.1 · statement 1/2 · read first

PROBLEM 13.1Evaporation from a drum

A bottle of pure $n$-heptane is accidentally poured into a drum of pure toluene in a laboratory. One of the laboratory assistants suggests that since heptane boils at a lower temperature than toluene, the following purification procedure can be used:

Pour the mixture (2 mol% $n$-heptane) into a simple still pot. Boil the mixture at 1 atm and condense the vapors until all heptane is boiled away. Obtain the pure toluene from the residue.

You, a chemical engineer with knowledge of vapor–liquid equilibrium, immediately realize that such a purification method will not work. (a) Indicate this by a curve showing the composition of the material remaining in the still pot after various quantities of the liquid have been distilled. What is the composition of the residue after 50 wt% of the original material has been distilled? What is the composition of the cumulative distillate? (b) When one-half of the heptane has been distilled, what is the composition of the cumulative distillate and the residue? What weight percent of the original material has been distilled?

Problem 13.2 · solution

PROBLEM 13.2Residue 0.057, distillate 0.547

(13-3) and (13-6)$\ln\dfrac{W}{W_0}=\displaystyle\int_{x_0}^{x}\dfrac{dx}{y-x},\qquad (x_D)_{avg}=\dfrac{W_0x_0-Wx}{W_0-W}$
$\ln\dfrac{W_0}{W}=\ln\dfrac{1}{0.3}=1.204$70 % vaporized: $W=0.3W_0$
$\displaystyle\int_{x}^{0.40}\frac{dx}{y-x}=1.204\ \Rightarrow\ x_W=0.057$monotone cubic through the 7.33 points
$(x_D)_{avg}=\dfrac{0.40-0.3(0.057)}{0.7}=0.547$(13-6), per mole of charge

First vapour is 0.580; the azeotrope (0.6854) caps any distillate.

Problem 13.3 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 13.3Differential distillation

A 30 mol% feed of benzene in toluene is to be distilled in a batch, differential-distillation operation. A product having an average composition of 45 mol% benzene is to be produced. Calculate the amount of residue, assuming $\alpha$ = 2.5 and $W_0$ = 100.

Fig. 13.1 Differential distillation

Problem 13.3 · solution

PROBLEM 13.3Residue: 57.4 mol at 0.189 benzene

(13-5) and (13-6)$\ln\dfrac{W_0}{W}=\dfrac{1}{\alpha-1}\left[\ln\dfrac{x_0}{x}+\alpha\ln\dfrac{1-x}{1-x_0}\right],\quad (x_D)_{avg}=\dfrac{W_0x_0-Wx}{W_0-W}$
$\dfrac{30-Wx}{100-W}=0.45$ with $W(x)$ from (13-5)two unknowns, two equations
$x=0.1887,\ W=57.4$solve by trial on $x$
$\dfrac{30-57.4(0.1887)}{42.6}=0.450$check the average
Residue 57.4 (per 100 charged), 18.9 mol% benzene; distillate 42.6 at 45 %.

Problem 13.7 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 13.7Differential distillation with added feed

A still pot is charged with 25 mol of benzene and toluene containing 35 mol% benzene. Feed of the same composition is supplied at a rate of 7 mol/h, and the heating rate is adjusted so that the liquid level in the still pot remains constant. If $\alpha$ = 2.5, how long will it be before the distillate composition falls to 45 mol% benzene?

Sketch: still pot with continuous feed

Problem 13.7 · solution

PROBLEM 13.7Constant level: 2.37 h

$W\dfrac{dx}{dt}=F\,(x_F-y),\qquad y=\dfrac{\alpha x}{1+(\alpha-1)x},\qquad D=F$

$F$ = feed rate, mol/h; $x_F$ = feed composition; $W$ constant.

$y=0.45\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{0.45}{2.5-1.5(0.45)}=0.2466$pot composition at the stop
$t=\displaystyle\int_{0.2466}^{0.35}\frac{25\,dx}{7\,(y-0.35)}=2.37\ \text{h}$separate and integrate numerically

Reachable: the pot only tends to $x$ = 0.177, where $y=x_F$.

Problem 13.8 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 13.8Differential distillation with continuous feed

A system consisting of a still pot and a total condenser is used to separate A and B from a trace of nonvolatile material. The still pot initially contains 20 lbmol of feed of 30 mol% A. Lecture 13-1 · summary

What section 13-1 settled

  • A simple still is one equilibrium stage; (13-3) links residue amount to composition.
  • Constant $\alpha$ integrates in closed form (13-5); tabulated VLE needs numerical area.
  • The receiver composition follows from a balance (13-6); time from $t=(W_0-W)/V$.
  • Purity needs high $\alpha$, so runs are cut: LK cut, slop cut, HK residue.

13-2

Lecture 13-2 · Binary batch rectification

What do a column and reflux buy a batch still — and how long does it take to collect the product?

Lecture 13-2 · the plan

Two ways to run a batch rectifier

  1. The rectifier and its three operating modesconstant reflux, constant distillate composition, optimal control
  2. Constant reflux on McCabe–ThieleSmoker–Rose: one operating-line slope, a moving start point
  3. Block's time and the average distillate(13-11) and (13-12); Example 13.4 by trial
  4. Constant distillate compositionBogart (13-13)–(13-18); Example 13.5, reflux rising with time
  5. Problems 13.9–13.17constant reflux and constant composition, hand-solved

13-2.1 · how long, and how pure on average

Block's time and the accumulated distillate

$\dfrac{dD}{dt}=V-L=V\left(1-\dfrac{L}{V}\right)$total balance on the condenser, constant boilup $V$
$t=\dfrac{W_0-W_t}{V\left(1-\frac{L}{V}\right)}=\dfrac{R+1}{V}\,(W_0-W_t)$(13-11)distillate collected equals charge lost
$x_{D_{avg}}=\dfrac{W_0x_0-W_tx_{W_t}}{W_0-W_t}$(13-12)LK balance: charge = residue + receiver

Constant $R$: instantaneous $x_D$ is above spec early, below it late.

13-2.2 · constant distillate composition (Bogart)

Fix $x_D$; let the reflux risestep 1 of 2

Constant $R$ lets purity drift. Hold $x_D$ fixed instead: the balance then needs no integral.

$W_0x_{W_0}=Wx_W+(W_0-W)\,x_D$LK balance; every drop left at $x_D$
$W=W_0\left[\dfrac{x_D-x_{W_0}}{x_D-x_W}\right]$(13-13)solve for the pot amount
$x_W=\dfrac{Wx_D-W_0\,(x_D-x_{W_0})}{W}$(13-14)or solve for the pot composition

Assumes negligible holdup and constant molar overflow; $L/V$ at each $x_W$ comes from McCabe–Thiele.

13-2.2 · constant distillate composition

Time for a schedule of $L/V$step 2 of 2

(13-13)$W=W_0\,(x_D-x_{W_0})/(x_D-x_W)$
$\dfrac{dW}{dt}=W_0\dfrac{(x_D-x_{W_0})}{(x_D-x_W)^2}\dfrac{dx_W}{dt}$(13-15)differentiate with $W$ and $x_W$ varying
$-\dfrac{dW}{dt}=V-L=\dfrac{dD}{dt}$(13-16)constant molar overflow; $D$ = amount collected
$t=\dfrac{W_0(x_D-x_{W_0})}{V}\displaystyle\int_{x_{W_t}}^{x_{W_0}}\frac{dx_W}{(1-L/V)(x_D-x_W)^2}$(13-17)substitute, separate, integrate

Rate: $dD/dt=V(1-L/V)$ (13-18); it falls as $L/V\to1$.

Example 13.5 · problem statement

EXAMPLE 13.5Constant Distillate Composition

A three-stage batch still (boiler and the equivalent of two equilibrium plates) is charged with 100 kmol of a liquid containing an equimolar mixture of $n$-hexane and $n$-octane. A liquid distillate of 0.9 mole-fraction hexane is to be maintained by continuously adjusting the reflux ratio, while maintaining a distillate rate of 20 kmol/h. What should the reflux ratio be after one hour when the accumulated distillate is 20 kmol? Theoretically, when must distillate accumulation be stopped? Assume negligible holdup and constant molar overflow.

Equilibrium curve of Fig. 13.7 (digitized, construction lines removed)

Example 13.5 · 3 stages, 100 kmol equimolar $n$C$_6$/$n$C$_8$, $x_D$ = 0.9, $D$ = 20 kmol/h

EXAMPLE 13.5Reflux after 1 h, and when to stop

(13-14) and the hexane balance$x_W=\dfrac{Wx_D-W_0(x_D-x_{W_0})}{W},\qquad W_0x_{W_0}=x_W\,W+x_D\,(W_0-W)$
$x_W=\dfrac{0.9(80)-100(0.9-0.5)}{80}=0.4$after 1 h: $D$ = 20 kmol, $W$ = 80
$L/V=0.22\ \Rightarrow\ R=\dfrac{0.22}{1-0.22}=0.282$3 steps from 0.4 to 0.9 (Fig. 13.7)
$0.06(100-20t)=50-20t(0.9)\ \Rightarrow\ t=\dfrac{44}{16.8}=2.62\ \text{h}$total reflux, $L/V$ = 1, leaves $x_W$ = 0.06

$t$ = time from the start of distillation, h; total reflux means $L/V=1$.

The book prints t = 2.58 h; its own equation solves to 2.62 h. Curve read off Fig. 13.7: $L/V$ = 0.25, total-reflux $x_W$ = 0.054.

Lecture 13-3 · Batch stripping, complex columns, liquid holdup

Can a batch column be fed from the top, or from the middle — and what does liquid held up in the column do to the cuts?

Lecture 13-3 · the plan

Other configurations, and the holdup caveat

  1. Batch strippercharge in an accumulator fed to the top; bottoms cuts (Fig. 13.8)
  2. Complex batch columnmiddle feed tank, products from both ends (Fig. 13.9)
  3. Which configuration for which taskmatching the charge and the wanted product to a layout
  4. Liquid holduptotal-reflux startup depletes the pot and delays the first cut

13-3 · Fig. 13.8

Batch stripping: the charge enters at the top

Fig. 13.8 Batch stripping

  • Charge sits in a large accumulator (feed tank), not the reboiler.
  • Fed to the top; cuts leave the bottom.
  • Removes small amounts of volatile impurities.
  • Binary: McCabe–Thiele tracks accumulator and bottoms.

13-3 · Fig. 13.9

Complex batch: feed tank at the middle

Fig. 13.9 Complex batch distillation

  • The feed tank charge enters at a suitable column location.
  • Cuts leave the condenser, the reboiler, or both.
  • Feed-point liquid may return to the tank to keep compositions close.
  • Result: considerable operating flexibility.

Interactive · pick a task

Which batch configuration fits the job?

The product's position sets the layout: overhead product → rectifier, bottoms product → stripper, both → complex column.

§13.4 · liquid holdup

Holdup matters when it exceeds a few percent of the charge

Sections 13-1 and 13-2 assumed no holdup. A real column starts at total reflux and fills its trays first.

At total-reflux startup

Trays and drum fill with LK-rich liquid; the pot becomes leaner. Initial purity and separation fall.

Over the run

Smaller product cuts, larger intermediate fractions, more residue, time and energy. Trays hold more than packing.

Interactive · dynamic tray model ($\alpha$ 2.5, 6 trays + drum, $R$ 4, $V$ 50 kmol/h, 100 kmol at 0.30)

Holdup depletes the pot before the first drop

Tray balance, constant holdup $M_j$$M_j\dfrac{dx_j}{dt}=Vy_{j-1}+Lx_{j+1}-Vy_j-Lx_j$

Total reflux until $x_D$ ≥ 0.98, then draw until $x_D$ < 0.95. Built for this deck.

$x_D$$x_W$0.5 % holdup

From 0.5 % to 15 % holdup, pot $x_W$ at first draw falls 0.30 → 0.22 and the draw starts 0.9 h later; the cut shrinks only 12.0 → 11.7 kmol.

Problem 13.20 · solution

PROBLEM 13.20Procedure: two sections, one feed tank

$\dfrac{d(M_Fx_F)}{dt}=-Dx_D-Bx_B,\qquad \dfrac{dM_F}{dt}=-D-B$

$M_F$, $x_F$ = feed-tank holdup, composition; $D$, $B$ = top and bottom draw rates.

rectifying: $y=\frac{L}{V}x+\left(1-\frac{L}{V}\right)x_D$step down from $x_D$ to the feed stage

match both at $x_F$; integrate the tank in timenew $x_D$, $x_B$ each step

Problem 13.21 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 13.21Effect of holdup on batch rectification

For a batch rectifier with appreciable column holdup: (a) Why is the charge to the still pot higher in the light component than at the start of rectification, assuming that total-reflux conditions are established before rectification? (b) Why will separation be more difficult than with zero holdup?

Fig. 13.10 Holdups $M_0$, $M_j$, $M_{N+1}$

Problem 13.21 · solution

PROBLEM 13.21Holdup stores light key before the first drop

(a) At total reflux the trays and drum fill with liquid rich in the light key; that light key came out of the pot, so the pot at the start of rectification is leaner than the original charge.
(b) The pot now starts with less light key, so the same stages give a lower initial distillate purity.

Problem 13.22 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 13.22Effect of holdup on batch rectification

For a batch rectifier with appreciable column holdup, why do tray compositions change less rapidly than they do for a rectifier with negligible column holdup, and why is the separation improved?

Fig. 13.10 Holdups $M_0$, $M_j$, $M_{N+1}$

Problem 13.22 · solution

PROBLEM 13.22Holdup acts as a flywheel

(13-24), one tray$\dfrac{dx_{i,j}}{dt}=\dfrac{L_{j-1}x_{i,j-1}-(L_j+K_{i,j}V_j)x_{i,j}+K_{i,j+1}V_{j+1}x_{i,j+1}}{M_j}$
Large $M_j$ divides the same flow imbalance: compositions drift slowly. The stored light-key-rich liquid keeps feeding reflux-like liquid downward, so sharp fronts survive longer and cuts separate better.

Problem 13.23 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 13.23Effect of holdup on batch rectification

Based on the statements in Exercises 13.21 and 13.22, why is it difficult to predict the effect of holdup?

Fig. 13.10 Holdups $M_0$, $M_j$, $M_{N+1}$

Problem 13.23 · solution

PROBLEM 13.23Two effects pull in opposite directions

Holdup depletes the pot at startup (13.21, worse) but damps composition changes (13.22, better). Net effect: case by case, with a rigorous model (§13.5).

The Lecture 13-3 holdup simulator shows both.

Lecture 13-3 · summary

What section 13-3 settled

  • Stripper: top feed from an accumulator, bottoms cuts; removes volatile traces.

§13.5.1 · rigorous model (Fig. 13.10)

Meadows, then Distefano: a column of mixed stages

  • Equilibrium, perfectly mixed stages.
  • No vapour holdup; constant molar liquid holdup $M$.
  • Adiabatic stages; partial reboiler, total condenser.
  • Total reflux first; distillate at fixed $D$, $R$ from $t=0$.

Result: differential-algebraic equations (DAEs), ordinary differential equations (ODEs) plus algebraic closures.

Fig. 13.10 Sections I–III (Distefano)

One ODE per component per stagestep 1 of 3

Specified: $N$, $D$, $R=L_0/D$, $M_{N+1}^0$, all $G_j$, plus correlations for $\rho$, $h$ and $K$.

§13.5.2 · two ways an integrator fails

Truncation error versus instability

Distefano compared 11 integrators on these equations. Two problems dominated, and only one shrinks politely with $\Delta t$.

Truncation error

Each step approximates the right-hand side. Local errors accumulate into global error; fewer significant digits. Smaller $\Delta t$ reduces it.

Instability

Results lose every significant digit. Shrinking $\Delta t$ does nothing until a method-specific limit is crossed; a smaller limit removes oscillations.

§13.5.2 · both first-order (Davis; Riggs)

Explicit and implicit Euler on $dy/dt=ay^2te^y$

$\dfrac{y_{k+1}-y_k}{\Delta t}=ay_k^2t_ke^{y_k}$(13-37)explicit: evaluate $f$ at the start of the step
$y_{k+1}=y_k+ay_k^2t_ke^{y_k}\,\Delta t$(13-38)solves directly, but $\Delta t$ is capped
$\dfrac{y_{k+1}-y_k}{\Delta t}=ay_{k+1}^2t_{k+1}e^{y_{k+1}}$(13-39)implicit: evaluate $f$ at the end; needs solving
$\Delta t_{max}\le\dfrac{2}{|\lambda|_{max}}$ (stable)    $\Delta t_{max}\le\dfrac{1}{|\lambda|_{max}}$ (no oscillation)

$k$ = step index; $\lambda$ = eigenvalue of the ODE Jacobian, h$^{-1}$. Implicit Euler is unconditionally stable.

§13.5.2 · stiffness (Gerschgorin estimate)

Small trays, big pot: a stiff system

(13-40), (13-41) from rows of (13-24), (13-25)$|\lambda|_{max}\approx2\dfrac{L_j+K_{i,j}V_j}{M_j},\quad |\lambda|_{min}\approx\dfrac{L_N+K_{i,N+1}V_{N+1}}{M_{N+1}}$
(13-42), $L$ = 10, $V$ = 20, $M^0_{N+1}$ = 100 kmol$\text{SR}\approx2\left(\dfrac{L+K_{lightest}V}{L+K_{heaviest}V}\right)\left(\dfrac{M^0_{N+1}}{M_{tray}}\right)$

Davis: 20 not stiff; 1,000 stiff; 1,000,000 very stiff.

Example 13.6 defaults give a stiffness ratio (SR) ≈ 31,700: stiff, so Gear-type implicit solvers (ODEPACK, MATLAB ode15s) are preferred.

§13.5.2 · modified Distefano procedure

Ten steps from total reflux to the last cut

Initialize (1–2)

Total reflux at $V^0_j$, $L^0_j$; then $L^0_j-D$

Time step (3–8)

Integrate implicitly, normalize, update $T_j$, $y$, $h$, $M$, flows

Iterate (9)

Repeat to the stop condition

New operation (10)

Dump receiver, change settings

Narrow-boiling feeds only; Boston et al.'s inside-out method handles wide-boiling, nonideal feeds.

Problem 13.26 · solution 1/2

PROBLEM 13.26Explicit Euler gives a negative mole fraction

(13-24), (13-27), $j$ = 2$\dfrac{dx_2}{dt}=\dfrac{L_1}{M_2}x_1-\dfrac{L_2+K_2V_2+\dfrac{dM_2}{dt}}{M_2}x_2+\dfrac{K_3V_3}{M_2}x_3,\quad \dfrac{dM_2}{dt}=V_3+L_1-V_2-L_2$
$dM_2/dt=209.5+157.5-209.0-158.0=0$(13-27)
$K_2=0.0449/0.0121=3.711,\ K_3=3.744$$K=y/x$ for benzene
$\dfrac{dx_2}{dt}=14{,}476(0.0276)-85{,}804(0.0121)+72{,}099(0.00884)=-1.33$coefficients in h$^{-1}$
$x_2(0.61)=0.0121+0.01(-1.33)=-0.0012$negative: unreasonable

Problem 13.26 · solution 2/2

PROBLEM 13.26Why: $\Delta t$ is 430 times too large

Explicit-Euler limits (13.5.2)$\Delta t\le 2/|\lambda|_{max},\quad |\lambda|_{max}\approx\dfrac{L_j+K_{i,j}V_j}{M_j}$ for that row
$|\lambda|\approx85{,}800$ h$^{-1}\Rightarrow\Delta t\le2.3\times10^{-5}$ hstage-2 diagonal coefficient
$66.4/0.01088\approx6{,}100$pot to tray holdup: slow and fast modes
0.01 h violates the stability limit; the system is stiff, so use an implicit (Gear-type) method.

Lecture 13-4 · summary

What section 13-4 settled

  • Distefano's model: $2CN+3C+4N+7$ equations; $C(N+2)$ component ODEs carry the dynamics.
  • Explicit Euler needs $\Delta t\le1/|\lambda|_{max}$: 2.86×10⁻⁴ h in Example 13.6.
  • Implicit Euler is stable at any step; truncation error limits it.
  • Small tray holdups make the system stiff (SR 31,700): use Gear-type solvers, as BatchSep and CC-BATCH do.

13-5

Lecture 13-5 · Intermediate cuts and optimal control

How should a campaign be cut, and its reflux scheduled, to get the most product in the least time?

Lecture 13-5 · the plan

Cut strategy, then reflux policy

  1. Luyben's two design aspectswhich products, and which control method
  2. Binary intermediate cut (Example 13.9)reflux ratio trades slop-cut size against time
  3. Ternary with two slop cuts (Example 13.10)termination specifications decide the cuts
  4. Optimal control (Example 13.11)constant $R$ vs constant $x_D$ vs an optimal $R(t)$
  5. Problems 13.30–13.31fewer slop cuts; pressure-controlled vaporization

§13.6 · intermediate-cut strategy (Luyben)

Design means choosing products and a control method

Simulators can now follow any campaign. The open question is which campaign to run.

Design parameters

Number of trays, charge size, boilup ratio, and the reflux ratio as a function of time.

Even a binary gives three products

LK-rich distillate, HK-rich residue, and an intermediate cut recycled to the next charge. A ternary may need more.

§13.7 · optimal control by varying $R$ (Diwekar)

Three objectives for one batch

Cuts fix what is collected. Reflux policy decides how fast and how much.

1

Maximum distillate

in a given time

2

Minimum time

for a given amount of distillate

3

Maximum profit

trading both

$R(t)$ is a function, not a number: calculus of variations, Pontryagin's maximum principle, dynamic programming or nonlinear programming.

PROBLEM 13.31Batch rectification at conditions of varying pressure

A hydrocarbon mixture comprised in mole fractions of, C$_3$H$_8$ = 0.1, $i$-C$_4$H$_{10}$ = 0.2, and a heavy component of average composition C$_{10}$H$_{22}$ = 0.70. is subject to batch vaporization at a constant temperature of 25°C and varying pressure until 1 mol% of the residue is $i$-C$_4$H$_{10}$. Determine the final pressure. What advantage might there be in controlling the vaporization by pressure rather than temperature?

Vapor pressure for the components at 25°C are:

ComponentVapor Pressure, mm Hg
C$_3$7,139
$i$-C$_4$2,611
C$_{10}$1.37

Sketch: isothermal flash-off by lowering pressure

Problem 13.31 · solution 1/2

PROBLEM 13.31Constant $T$ makes $\alpha$ exactly constant

(13-10), Raoult at fixed $T$$\dfrac{M_i}{M_{i_0}}=\left(\dfrac{M_j}{M_{j_0}}\right)^{\alpha_{i,j}},\qquad \alpha_{i,j}=\dfrac{P_i^s}{P_j^s}$
$\alpha_{C3}=7139/1.37=5211,\ \alpha_{iC4}=1906$reference $j$ = C$_{10}$
$\dfrac{20f^{1906}}{70f+20f^{1906}+10f^{5211}}=0.01$$f=M_{C10}/70$ in 100 mol
$f=0.99825$: 0.71 mol $i$-C$_4$, 0.001 mol C$_3$ leftonly 0.12 mol C$_{10}$ vaporizes

Problem 13.31 · solution 2/2

PROBLEM 13.31Final pressure 27.6 mmHg

Bubble point of the residue$P=\sum_i x_iP_i^s$
$P=0.00002(7139)+0.0100(2611)+0.98998(1.37)$residue: 70.58 mol
$P=27.6$ mmHgfrom 1,237 mmHg at the start
Pressure control keeps the heavy residue at 25°C: no heating of C$_{10}$, no thermal degradation, and fast, cheap control via the vacuum.

Lecture 13-5 · summary

What section 13-5 settled

  • Higher $R$ shrinks the intermediate cut but lengthens the run, by (13-11).
  • Ternary feeds need termination triggers per cut, and may need two slop cuts.
  • Constant $x_D$ beat constant $R$ by 2.6 % in Example 13.11.
  • An optimal $R(t)$ lies between the two and gains most on hard separations.

Chapter 13 · what to keep

Key Takeaways

1

Integrate Rayleigh, $\ln(W/W_0)=\int dx/(y-x)$, for any simple-still question.

2

Get averages from balances, (13-6) and (13-12), never from integrals.

3

Time a constant-$R$ run with $t=(R+1)(W_0-W_t)/V$.

4

Check $\Delta t\le1/|\lambda|_{max}$ before trusting an explicit integration.

5

Trade slop-cut size against time with $R$; let reflux rise for more product.
